pedagogy.summary: Direct comparison of length or height means putting two objects together and judging which has more — and the whole skill hinges on ALIGNING one endpoint before comparing the other. Length is the distance between an object's two endpoints (CCSS Progression), so a fair comparison needs a common starting line. Children who have not grasped this judge by which object 'sticks out farthest' or by which top is higher, ignoring where each object begins. Back-to-back height comparison is an easy entry because standing on the same floor aligns one endpoint automatically — but that very automaticity hides the alignment move, so it must be made explicit with staggered and raised cases.
bestPractices: Make endpoint alignment the explicit heart of the lesson: line up two objects at a common starting line, THEN compare the far ends
Use a 'mixed-up' puppet (Mr MixUp) who compares without lining up the starting ends, so children catch and correct the endpoint error themselves
Start with back-to-back / side-by-side aligned comparisons, then deliberately stagger the objects and raise one (a tower on a book) so children must attend to the base, not just the top
Build precise comparative language in the moment — longer/shorter, taller/shorter — rather than the global 'bigger'
Address conservation with rotate-and-restore and bend-and-straighten demonstrations: 'it looks longer now, but it really isn't' — show, don't just tell
Give indirect-comparison bridges later (string as a go-between) but keep this stage on fair DIRECT comparison with aligned ends
keyRepresentations: Two ribbons/pencils lined up against a common starting line, far ends compared
A 'mixed-up' puppet placing objects unaligned for the child to fix
Two towers, one raised on a book, prompting attention to a common base
Equal-length strips, one rotated vertical or bent into a curve, to confront non-conservation
commonMisconceptions: Judging by one endpoint — picks the object that 'sticks out farthest' at one end without aligning the starting ends
Ignoring the baseline for height — calls the tower whose top is higher 'taller' even though it stands on a book and has fewer blocks
Non-conservation — believes an object becomes longer when turned vertical, or that a ribbon becomes shorter when curved because its endpoints move closer
Using undifferentiated 'bigger' instead of the specific comparative word (longer/taller), signalling the length attribute is not yet differentiated

learn.summary: Teaches young children (roughly ages 4–6) to compare two objects directly by length or height, with endpoint alignment as the explicit heart of the skill: line up one end at a common starting line, THEN compare the far ends. Addresses the classic errors of judging by whichever end 'sticks out farthest', ignoring a raised baseline for height, and non-conservation (believing length changes when an object is bent or rotated). Builds precise comparative language (longer/shorter, taller/shorter) rather than the global 'bigger'.

activities.title: Line up the ends, then compare (ribbons)
feedback: If the child picks the ribbon poking out while the near ends are unaligned, don't just mark it wrong: have them align the starting ends and look again — because the other (actually longer) ribbon was shifted back, once the starts match it runs further past the finish
Prompt 'where does each one START?' to direct attention to the near endpoints
Use the mixed-up puppet so the child spots and corrects the endpoint error themselves rather than being told
activities.rationale: Length is how far an object extends along itself from one end to the other (for a straight object, from endpoint to endpoint), so a fair direct comparison of two straightened objects needs a common starting line. Children at the Length Direct Comparer level physically align two objects at one endpoint before comparing the others; a mixed-up puppet is a documented way to surface the alignment error. Staggering the pair forces the alignment judgement that a pre-aligned (back-to-back) comparison would do for the child.
sourceClaims: Kindergartners easily compare lengths when objects stand next to each other because that automatically aligns one endpoint (back-to-back height comparison), but in other situations may compare only one endpoint and point to the object that 'sticks out the farthest'; teachers should reinforce the necessity of aligning endpoints (e.g. the pencil-reveal 'were you fooled?'). Length may not be conserved — children may think a stick turned vertical is now longer, or a bent string is now shorter.

At the Length Direct Comparer level a child physically aligns two objects at one endpoint and then compares the other endpoints, using long/longer/longest; instruction focuses on lining objects up at one endpoint before comparing, and notes that in back-to-back height comparison the feet endpoint is aligned for the child so the alignment step often goes unrecognised. A mixed-up puppet is used to surface the endpoint-alignment error.
learnerActions: Look at two ribbons lying staggered on the table, with the SHORTER ribbon shifted so its right end pokes out past the longer ribbon's right end and the near ends left unaligned
Say which ribbon is longer and explain how you know
Either slide both ribbons to a common starting line, or (in a non-draggable image) draw a line to mark the common start, then compare the far ends again
Meet a 'mixed-up' puppet (e.g. Mr MixUp) who compares WITHOUT lining up the starting ends; catch and fix the puppet's mistake
Answer: 'Where does each ribbon START? Put your finger on the beginning of each one.'
activities.intendedInsight: To compare fairly, line up one end of each object at a common start; then the far ends show which is longer. Looking at the far ends tells you nothing reliable while the starting ends are not matched. The object that 'sticks out' at one end is not automatically the longer one.

activities.title: Compare towers from a common base
feedback: If the child says the book-raised tower is taller because its top is higher, guide them to notice it has fewer of the same-sized blocks and starts raised, then bring both to the same surface and compare
Make explicit: 'we compare from where each one STARTS (the base), not just the top'
activities.rationale: Back-to-back/standing comparisons align the base automatically, which hides the alignment move; deliberately raising one object on a book makes the baseline judgement necessary and visible. This parallels endpoint alignment for length, applied to height.
sourceClaims: Kindergartners easily compare lengths when objects stand next to each other because that automatically aligns one endpoint (back-to-back height comparison), but in other situations may compare only one endpoint and point to the object that 'sticks out the farthest'; teachers should reinforce the necessity of aligning endpoints (e.g. the pencil-reveal 'were you fooled?'). Length may not be conserved — children may think a stick turned vertical is now longer, or a bent string is now shorter.
learnerActions: Look at two towers built from identical blocks: a taller tower (more blocks) standing on the floor, and a shorter tower (fewer blocks) standing on a thick book so its TOP is higher
Say which tower is taller and explain how you know
Bring the book-raised tower down onto the floor (or reason explicitly about the book's height) so both start from the same surface, then compare again
Try a harder case: raise the shorter tower even higher on two books — 'now is it taller? What if I put it on the floor?'
activities.intendedInsight: To compare heights fairly, both objects must start from a common base; you cannot judge just by where the tops are. Here the shorter tower looks taller only because it sits on a book; move both to the same surface to compare fairly.

activities.title: Does length change when you bend it? (conservation)
feedback: If the child says the straight ribbon is now longer than the curved one, do NOT mark it wrong or drill it: narrate 'it looks longer now, but it really isn't', straighten the ribbon, and let them check
Let the child predict first, then restore the shape to confirm — show, don't just tell
activities.rationale: Non-conservation of length is developmental: children may judge length by how far apart the endpoints look, so a curved ribbon seems shorter and a vertical stick seems longer. Conservation emerges with maturation and experience, so repeated predict-then-check bend-and-straighten / rotate-and-restore demonstrations are more appropriate than correction or drilling.
sourceClaims: Kindergartners easily compare lengths when objects stand next to each other because that automatically aligns one endpoint (back-to-back height comparison), but in other situations may compare only one endpoint and point to the object that 'sticks out the farthest'; teachers should reinforce the necessity of aligning endpoints (e.g. the pencil-reveal 'were you fooled?'). Length may not be conserved — children may think a stick turned vertical is now longer, or a bent string is now shorter.
learnerActions: Look at two ribbons of exactly equal length; one is then bent into a wavy curve
Predict: 'are they still the same length, or is one longer now?'
Watch (or press 'straighten') as the curved ribbon is straightened back out, and check the prediction
Try the rotate version: an equal stick turned vertical — predict whether it 'got longer', then restore it to compare
activities.intendedInsight: Length does not change just because an object is bent or turned — a bent ribbon is the same length when straightened; a stick is the same length lying down or standing up (though how tall it stands does depend on which way it is turned).

activities.title: Say it precisely: longer, shorter, taller
feedback: If the child points to the correct object but calls it 'bigger', name the specific attribute and its comparative word tied to the length/height question before more practice
Gently correct loose mixing of longer/shorter/taller by tying each word to what is being compared
activities.rationale: Using undifferentiated 'bigger' signals the length attribute is not yet separated from global size; KS1 expectations include comparing and describing lengths and heights with vocabulary such as long/short, longer/shorter, tall/short. Building the comparative word in the moment of comparison supports attribute differentiation.
sourceClaims: KS1 pupils should compare, describe and solve practical problems for lengths and heights and measure lengths/heights, using vocabulary such as long/short, longer/shorter, tall/short, double/half.
learnerActions: After each comparison, describe the result with the specific comparative word — 'this ribbon is LONGER', 'this tower is TALLER' — not just 'bigger'
Match the word to the attribute: longer/shorter for length laid out, taller/shorter for height standing up
Describe practical real-object pairs (two pencils, two strips) using long/short, longer/shorter, tall/short
activities.intendedInsight: Length and height are specific attributes with specific words; naming them precisely shows you are comparing the right thing, not just overall 'size'.

constraints: Pre-aligned comparisons (back-to-back, side-by-side at a common start) can be passed WITHOUT understanding, because the alignment is done for the child; include staggered pairs and a raised tower so the child must perform the alignment/baseline judgement.

A static picture or tap-to-reveal image can show aligned vs unaligned pairs and reveal the correct answer, but the child does not physically slide objects into alignment — the core action is demonstrated rather than done. Treat such images as a scaffold toward hands-on or draggable aligning.

A recognition-only selection task ('which is longer?') scores the alignment judgement but does not let the child perform the physical align action with live feedback — recognition alone does not elicit the aligning action; a draw-a-line-to-align step adds a construction element, though still short of free manipulation.
Non-conservation is developmental: do not mark it wrong or drill it. Provide repeated predict-then-check demonstrations and let conservation emerge with experience.
Keep this stage on fair DIRECT comparison with aligned ends; indirect-comparison bridges (e.g. using a string as a go-between) belong to a later stage.
Build precise comparative language (longer/shorter, taller/shorter) rather than the global 'bigger'.

Real objects have thickness and sit on surfaces; the alignment idea is about the endpoints/base. When using an on-screen model, treat it as a representation of the physical lining-up action, not a replacement for it where hands-on tools are expected.
Double/half language appears in the curriculum statement but is beyond simple direct comparison; introduce only when ready and do not conflate it with longer/shorter judgements.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The original flagged the UK National Curriculum (KS1) source as unverified (verified:false); treat the double/half and vocabulary claim accordingly.

The source row's artefact-fit notes asserted that a 3D back-to-back view 'adds little' and that a conversation 'cannot render' the comparison. These are catalog-fit opinions, not established efficacy claims; retained only as scope observations, not universal laws. A spoken/role interaction could still support reasoning aloud even if it does not itself provide the object to align.

Optional interactive mechanisms from the original design (drag two ribbons to a start line; a near-end alignment marker; far-end comparison that 'lights up' only when aligned; a Mr MixUp mode; slide-tower-off-a-book; a 'straighten' button for the conservation case) are preserved as example feedback mechanisms, not mandatory requirements.

One misconception (undifferentiated 'bigger') links to a prerequisite micro-topic on the underlying attribute distinction; reteaching that attribute distinction may be needed before precise-vocabulary practice.

The LearningTrajectories 'Length Direct Comparer' claim supports endpoint alignment (activities 1 and 2) but does not address conservation; it is therefore attached only to the alignment activity and excluded from the conservation activity's sourceClaims, which rests on the CCSS conservation statement only.

probeDeeper: 'Where does each ribbon START? Put your finger on the beginning of each one.' (surfaces whether the child attends to the near endpoints)
Counterexample: raise the SHORTER tower even higher on two books — 'now is it taller? What if I put it on the floor?' (tests baseline reasoning against a stronger illusion)
'You said this straight one is longer than the curly one. Watch — I'll straighten the curly one. Now which is longer?' (confronts non-conservation with a restore)
'Show me a fair way to check which of these two pencils is longer.' (checks the child can set up aligned direct comparison independently)
assess.correctAnswer: (1) Lines up one end of both ribbons at a common starting line, then compares the far ends, and names the genuinely longer ribbon (not the one that was poking out). (2) Compares from a common base — recognises the book-raised tower only looks taller, brings both to the same surface or reasons about the book's height, and identifies the tower with more actual height. (3) Says the two ribbons are still the same length even though one is now curved — length is conserved when a ribbon is bent.

errorPatterns.pattern: Judges by one endpoint — picks whichever object 'sticks out farthest' at one end without lining up the starting ends
errorPatterns.nextMove: Line up both objects at one end first, then compare the other ends; use the mixed-up puppet who forgets to align so the child spots and fixes the error; ask 'where does each one START?'
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task 1 chooses the shorter ribbon because its far end protrudes; does not move the ribbons to a common start

errorPatterns.pattern: Ignores the baseline for height — calls the tower with the higher top 'taller' regardless of the raised base
errorPatterns.nextMove: Bring both towers to the same surface before comparing tops; discuss that height is measured from a common base, not from wherever the object happens to stand.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task 2 says the tower on the book is taller because its top is higher, even though it has fewer blocks and starts raised

errorPatterns.pattern: Non-conservation — believes length changes when an object is rotated or bent (a curved ribbon is 'shorter' because its ends are closer; a vertical stick is 'longer' than the same stick horizontal)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT mark it wrong or drill it — conservation emerges with maturation and experience. Provide repeated bend-and-straighten and rotate-and-restore demonstrations, narrating 'it looks longer, but it really isn't', and let the child predict then check.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task 3 says the straight ribbon is now longer than the curved one; judges length by how far apart the endpoints look

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses undifferentiated 'bigger' instead of the specific comparative word, signalling the length attribute is not yet separated from global size
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach the underlying attribute distinction: name the specific attribute and its comparative word ('longer', 'taller') tied to the length question, before precise-vocabulary practice.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Correctly points to the longer object but calls it 'bigger', or mixes longer/shorter/taller loosely

responseLevels.gap: Judges by a single protruding end or by which top is higher regardless of the base; cannot reliably line objects up; believes length changes when a ribbon is bent.
responseLevels.full: Spontaneously aligns one endpoint (or equalises the base) before comparing the far ends across staggered and raised cases, holds length invariant under rotation and bending, and describes the result with precise comparative language (longer/shorter/taller).
responseLevels.partial: Compares correctly when objects are already side by side at a common start (back-to-back), but is fooled by staggered ribbons or a raised tower, and/or does not yet conserve length under bending/rotation.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set three tasks and WATCH — do not explain the method first. (1) Lay two ribbons of different lengths on the table STAGGERED: shift the SHORTER ribbon forward so its far end sticks out past the longer one's far end, and leave the near ends unaligned. Ask 'which ribbon is longer? Show me how you know.' (2) Build two block towers — one taller tower on the floor, and a shorter tower standing on a thick book so its TOP is higher. Ask 'which tower is taller?' (3) Take two ribbons of exactly equal length; bend one into a wavy curve. Ask 'are they still the same length, or is one longer now?' Watch whether the child aligns the starting ends, accounts for the raised base, and conserves length.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Pre-aligned comparisons (back-to-back) can be passed without understanding, because the alignment is done for the child. Staggering the ribbons and raising one tower forces the alignment/baseline judgement: a child who judges by a single protruding end picks the shorter ribbon, and one who judges by 'highest top' picks the raised tower — both tells. The conservation item separates children who believe length changes with shape from those who hold it invariant.
